title: The Pomegranate, the Apple-Tree, and the Bramble
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Pomegranate and an Apple-tree were disputing about the quality of their fruits, and each claimed that its own was the better of the two. High words passed between them, and a violent quarrel was imminent, when a Bramble impudently poked its head out of a neighbouring hedge and said, "There, that's enough, my friends; don't let us quarrel."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what were the Pomegranate and the Apple-tree disputing about?
options: Which one flowered first each year

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did each of them claim about its own fruit?
options: That it was the better of the two
That it grew in greater numbers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what seemed about to happen between the Pomegranate and the Apple-tree?
According to the passage, where did the Bramble poke its head out from?
According to the passage, what does the Bramble say to the Pomegranate and the Apple-tree?
options: "That's enough, my friends; don't let us quarrel"
"I will judge which of you is right"

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "disputing" mean in "were disputing about the quality of their fruits"?
As the passage uses it, what does "impudently" mean in "a Bramble impudently poked its head out"?
Based on the passage, why is it notable that the Bramble is the one who speaks up and calls the two "my friends"?
options: The Bramble is actually a close relative of both plants
A lowly, fruitless plant is presuming to referee a dispute between two plants prized for their fruit
The Bramble had won a similar argument before
The Bramble was asked by both sides to settle the matter

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who interrupts the quarrel between the Pomegranate and the Apple-tree?
According to the passage, what passed between the Pomegranate and the Apple-tree before the Bramble spoke?
According to the passage, what two plants are arguing over the quality of their fruits?
As the passage uses it, what does "imminent" mean in "a violent quarrel was imminent"?
Based on the passage, what makes the Bramble's plea for peace come across as absurd?
options: The Bramble has no fruit of its own worth comparing, yet acts as if it stands as an equal to the two quarrelling trees
The Bramble is actually causing the quarrel itself
The Bramble has already been asked to leave the hedge
The Bramble agrees that the Apple-tree's fruit is best

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Pomegranate and an Apple-tree nearly come to a quarrel over whose fruit is better, until an unworthy Bramble presumes to call for peace between them as an equal
A Bramble challenges a Pomegranate and an Apple-tree to grow better fruit
A Pomegranate and an Apple-tree agree the Bramble's berries are the finest of all
A Bramble settles a quarrel by proving its own fruit is best
